issues.description: The problem statement and UML specify a Meal class (with name and ingredients and corresponding getters), and the solution repository provides Meal.java. However, the template repository's Meal.java is empty while it contains an Order.java implementing the same fields/constructor/getters. This naming/structure mismatch in the template (Order vs. Meal) will confuse students and block them from implementing the exercise as described (tests and instructions expect a Meal class).
issues.suggestedFix: Provide a proper Meal.java in the template that matches the problem description (name, ingredients, constructor, and getters). Remove or rename the template Order.java (or clearly explain its presence) so students are not misled. For example, copy the Order.java implementation into Meal.java (or rename Order.java to Meal.java) and update any template Main comments to reference Meal. Ensure the template's class names match the UML/problem statement and the tests' expectations.

issues.description: The problem statement and the solution repository refer to the core domain entity as 'Meal' (including a Meal class and Meal[] orders), but the template repository provides an 'Order' class (src/de/tum/cit/ase/Order.java) instead of a 'Meal' class. This mismatch (Meal vs Order) is the same conceptual entity represented with different identifiers across artifacts and can confuse students trying to map the exercise requirements to the starter code and expected solution.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the identifier across artifacts. Update the template to provide a Meal class (rename Order.java to Meal.java and adjust references in Main and other starter code) so the starter code, problem statement, and solution consistently use 'Meal'. Alternatively, if 'Order' is intended, update the problem statement and solution to use 'Order' consistently or add a clear note in the template explaining that Order in the starter code corresponds to Meal in the specification.
